title: Run a Money Meeting That Ends in Decisions
meta_description: Use a structured couples money meeting to align cash flow, debt, accounts, goals, autonomy and follow-through without blame or financial control.

module_headings.external_sources: Primary Conversation, Banking and Tax Guidance

sections.heading: A Money Meeting Is Not a Financial Ambush
paragraphs: A useful money meeting is a scheduled decision session between partners, not a surprise audit of one person’s character. Its purpose is to create shared visibility, choose a small number of actions and assign follow-through. If the conversation ends only with emotion or a larger spreadsheet, the operating problem remains.

Ask for the meeting rather than announcing it during a purchase dispute. Offer a bounded time, neutral place and draft agenda that either partner can change. Avoid starting when someone is hungry, rushing, caring for children, exhausted or already activated by another conflict.

[[S1|The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau’s conversation tool]] recommends preparing goals, decisions and documents in advance. That structure matters because money carries memories about scarcity, status, safety, family and control. A process creates room for those meanings without letting them replace facts.

Begin with a shared statement: “We are here to understand the same household and make the next month easier.” Do not open with a list of errors. Use account and transaction language instead of moral labels such as irresponsible, cheap, secretive or controlling.

The opening photograph shows a couple writing beside a calculator and laptop because productive meetings combine attention with records. Neither person should be forced to defend every transaction from memory while the other holds all the data.

Agree on meeting rules: no insults, threats, interruptions, device distractions or unilateral account changes; either person can request a pause; unresolved items get a return date. These are operational safeguards, not attempts to make disagreement disappear.

Separate discovery from judgment. The first session may reveal an unknown subscription, tax balance, family obligation or irregular income. Record it accurately before deciding what it means. Immediate accusation can teach a partner that disclosure is punished.

Do not require identical money personalities. One person may value certainty while another values flexibility; one may prefer detail while another wants a dashboard. The system should protect shared commitments and leave agreed personal discretion, not declare one temperament correct.

If there is intimidation, monitoring, coerced debt, blocked access to money or fear of retaliation, a joint meeting may be unsafe. Seek confidential legal, financial or domestic-violence support and protect device and account security. Collaboration advice must never pressure someone to disclose into danger.

The first meeting succeeds when both partners know why they are there, can add agenda items and leave with no more than a few named decisions. Trust grows from accurate follow-through, not from a promise to “communicate better.”

Decide what the meeting will not cover. Parenting disputes, old relationship injuries and every discretionary purchase cannot all be resolved inside one financial agenda. Note connected issues and schedule the appropriate conversation or support. Protecting scope keeps the meeting from becoming a container for every unresolved grievance and makes it more likely that both partners will agree to return.
Keep the process mutual and specific.

sections.heading: Prepare One Shared Snapshot Without Sharing Every Password
paragraphs: Each partner should gather information before the session: take-home income, irregular income, account balances, debt balances and rates, recurring bills, insurance, retirement contributions, tax notices and the next ninety days of unusual expenses. Use statements, not estimates, when available.

Create a household inventory with institution, account type, legal owner, beneficiary where relevant, purpose, balance, minimum payment, due date and access owner. Inventory is not permission to publish credentials. Never place passwords, full account numbers or identity documents in an ordinary shared spreadsheet.

[[S2|The CFPB advises couples]] to know the family’s accounts, property, income, bills, insurance and important contacts so responsibility can shift during illness or emergency. Shared awareness is different from giving both people unlimited transactional authority.

List ownership precisely: individual, joint, authorized user, beneficiary, trustee, business or retirement account. A person who can see or use an account may not own it, and a beneficiary does not control it during the owner’s life. Verify the institution agreement and local law for important decisions.

For each monthly bill, record amount range, due date, payment method, source account, autopay status and responsible reviewer. Include annual and quarterly bills by converting them into sinking-fund amounts. The household should not appear balanced only because irregular expenses were omitted.

Use the same measurement date for balances. A checking balance before rent and a card balance after payment can create a false cash picture. Mark pending transactions, reimbursements and transfers so they are not counted twice.

Disclose material debts, guarantees, tax liabilities and family commitments. The goal is not forced confession of every past choice; it is preventing an obligation that affects shared cash from remaining invisible. Set a threshold for what “material” means and apply it to both partners.

Keep personal safety and autonomy intact. Partners can share summaries and statements without exchanging every login. Use institution-supported joint access, authorized roles, password managers and emergency documents rather than texting credentials or reusing passwords.

Bring one to three personal goals and one to three household goals. A meeting built only around problems becomes punitive. Goals reveal why the cash-flow changes matter and where each person needs room rather than restriction.

The preparation step is complete when the couple can answer what money arrives, what must leave, what is owned or owed, who can act and which facts remain uncertain. Mark uncertainty instead of filling it with assumptions.

Check whose name receives each statement and alert. If all records flow to one inbox or phone, the other partner can be excluded unintentionally even when accounts are shared. Add institution-supported read access, duplicate notices or a secure household document routine. Continuity should not depend on one person remaining available, healthy and willing to translate the entire system.

sections.heading: Use an Agenda That Moves from Facts to Decisions
paragraphs: A reliable agenda follows a sequence: check-in, changes since last meeting, current balances, upcoming bills, exceptions, one priority decision, assigned actions and next date. Put emotionally difficult items after the shared snapshot but before everyone is fatigued.

Start with a two-minute check-in. Each person names one financial win, one concern and one desired outcome. This prevents the person who speaks fastest from defining the meeting and creates a record of progress as well as problems.

Review only the indicators needed to make decisions: operating-account balance, bills before next income, card statement totals, reserve balance, priority-goal progress and exceptions. A thirty-tab workbook can hide a missed utility bill as effectively as no budget.

Use an exception list instead of inspecting every ordinary purchase. Exceptions include an overdraft, missed payment, spending beyond an agreed threshold, income shortfall, unusual fee or delayed transfer. Ask what changed in the system before blaming motive.

Limit the agenda to one major decision when the topic is complex: debt order, account structure, housing change, family support or benefit enrollment. Smaller operational items can be handled together, but multiple identity-level debates produce weak decisions.

Define the decision before discussing solutions. “We need to free $400 monthly by January without missing debt minimums” is testable. “You spend too much” is not. Write constraints such as safety, childcare, work needs, minimum reserves and contractual payments.

Generate at least two options and show their household effects. A spending cut, added income, timeline change or smaller goal can solve the same gap differently. Include whose time and labor each option consumes; unpaid coordination is a real resource.

Use a parking lot for tax, legal, investment or relationship questions needing outside help. Assign the research owner, source and return date. Do not force a false answer to achieve closure before the meeting ends.
Close by reading decisions aloud: amount, account, owner, deadline and verification. Schedule the next session before leaving. Verbal agreement without an implementation owner is a hope, not a plan.

The agenda passes when it is short enough to finish, broad enough to show the household and specific enough to produce actions. It should lower uncertainty between meetings rather than create a new weekly trial.

Assign a facilitator and note-taker for the session, then rotate those roles. The facilitator protects time and sequence rather than controlling the outcome. The note-taker records decisions, not a transcript of vulnerable comments. Rotation prevents meeting mechanics from becoming another invisible job permanently attached to the more financially confident partner.

Put a hard stop ten minutes before the scheduled end. Use that time to choose among decide, delegate, research or defer for each open item. A topic is not resolved merely because time expired. Naming its status prevents unfinished work from returning later as an accusation that the other person ignored an agreement that was never actually made.

sections.heading: Build Cash Flow Around Dates, Not Monthly Averages
paragraphs: A couple can have enough income for the month and still miss bills when pay dates and due dates do not align. Build a week-by-week cash-flow view showing opening balance, income date, essential bills, debt minimums, planned saving and a minimum operating buffer.

[[S3|FDIC Money Smart]] distinguishes a spending and saving plan from guesswork by listing net income, expenses and saving. Use actual recent transactions to establish the baseline, then adjust for the coming month instead of treating last month as a rule.

Divide expenses into obligations, essentials, flexible shared spending, personal spending, sinking funds and goals. Categories should support decisions, not carry shame. Groceries and childcare can vary; mark a realistic range rather than choosing an aspirational number that fails immediately.

Identify bills with serious consequences first: housing, utilities, insurance, required transport, taxes, child support and debt secured by essential assets. When money is short, investigate hardship options and professional guidance early rather than paying the loudest caller automatically.

Create sinking funds for predictable irregular costs such as vehicle maintenance, annual insurance, school, travel, holidays, medical deductibles and home repair. Divide the expected amount by remaining pay periods and revisit when evidence changes.

Choose an operating buffer below which discretionary transfers pause. A buffer protects timing errors and small surprises; it is not the full emergency fund. Both partners should know when it can be used and how it is restored.

Automate stable obligations only after confirming amount, date and source balance. Autopay prevents some missed payments but can also trigger overdrafts when income is irregular. Add calendar reminders before large debits and review the statement after payment.

The midpoint photograph shows a couple under stress because timing problems often feel personal. The intervention is to slow the conversation, name the cash date causing pressure and choose an operational fix. Visible distress is a pause signal, not evidence that one person has won.

For irregular income, build the base plan from a conservative floor and direct surplus through a written waterfall: catch up essential obligations, restore buffer, fund taxes, reduce priority debt and advance goals. Do not commit volatile income twice.
The cash-flow section passes when every bill before the next meeting has a source, known gaps have an owner and neither partner must guess whether the shared account can support an ordinary purchase.

Reconcile transfers between household accounts so they do not appear as income or spending twice. Credit-card payments are cash movements against earlier purchases, not new expenses when the purchases were already categorized. A clean method matters because false double counting can manufacture a conflict over money that the household never actually spent.

sections.heading: Discuss Debt as a Contract, Not a Character Trait
paragraphs: Prepare a debt table with creditor, legal borrower, current balance, interest rate, minimum, due date, promotional expiration, collateral and delinquency status. Separate joint debt, individual debt and authorized-user accounts. Responsibility depends on contract and law, not household shorthand.

Pull credit reports through the authorized source and review them individually. A partner should not impersonate the other or demand credentials. Compare reports with the shared inventory and dispute errors through the appropriate process.

Decide the payoff objective: minimize interest, remove a dangerous secured debt, resolve delinquency, improve cash flow or simplify accounts. The mathematically cheapest order may not address the most urgent legal or household consequence.

Keep all required minimums current while directing extra money to the chosen target, unless a qualified hardship or legal plan says otherwise. Record the extra amount and expected review date rather than making a vague commitment to “pay more.”

When one partner entered the relationship with debt, distinguish legal liability from the couple’s chosen support. Partners can agree to use shared resources without rewriting ownership. Document the agreement and revisit it if income or relationship status changes.

Do not consolidate merely to reduce the number of payments. Compare interest, fees, term, collateral, variable rates, lost protections and total repayment. Turning unsecured debt into debt secured by a home can increase the consequence of failure.

Set a borrowing rule: which purchases can use credit, the amount requiring discussion, who may apply, and whether the balance must be paid by a date. A shared goal does not authorize one person to open credit in the other’s name.

Watch for promotional rates and deferred-interest terms. Add the end date to the household calendar and calculate the payment required to finish before it. A minimum shown on the statement may not meet that target.

If collections, tax debt, lawsuits, repossession or foreclosure are possible, seek reputable legal or nonprofit counseling promptly. A money meeting cannot negotiate rights it does not understand. Record contacts and documents, not improvised promises.

The debt section succeeds when every material obligation is visible, legal responsibility is accurate, the next payment is funded and extra dollars follow one agreed rule. Shame does not reduce principal; a verified process can.

Review credit-card roles separately: primary borrower, joint borrower and authorized user can have different liability and credit-report effects. Removing a card from a wallet does not close an account or end contractual responsibility. Confirm changes with the issuer, preserve statements and consider credit-report impact before closing an established account solely to signal progress.

sections.heading: Choose an Account Structure That Balances Access and Autonomy
paragraphs: Joint, separate and hybrid banking can all work. The test is whether the structure funds shared obligations, preserves agreed autonomy, provides emergency continuity and matches legal ownership. Combining everything is not proof of trust; separating everything is not proof of secrecy.

A hybrid system can route agreed contributions into a joint operating account while each partner retains individual spending or saving accounts. Contribution formulas can be equal dollars, proportional income or another arrangement reflecting caregiving and household labor. Write the rule and review it.

[[S4|The CFPB notes]] that in most circumstances either owner of a joint checking account can withdraw funds and close the account, subject to agreement and law. A joint account is a legal access decision, not merely a shared budgeting folder.

Define personal discretionary money that does not require transaction-by-transaction approval. The amount should fit the plan and apply fairly. Autonomy reduces surveillance and lets gifts, hobbies and ordinary preferences exist without reopening the household budget.

Shared visibility still matters. Both partners should know the operating account, bill calendar, reserves, insurance and major assets or debts even when one handles administration. The backup partner should be able to keep housing, utilities and insurance current during illness.

Avoid granting joint ownership solely for convenience. Authorized signers, convenience accounts, powers of attorney and trusted contacts have different rights and consequences. Obtain institution and legal guidance before adding someone to an account or title.

Update beneficiaries and payable-on-death instructions separately from account access. Marriage alone does not guarantee every designation matches the estate plan. Retirement, insurance and transfer-on-death forms require direct review.

Protect credentials. Use individual logins where institutions support them, multifactor authentication and secure recovery methods. Do not use one partner’s identity to access an account if the institution has not authorized that role.

Document what happens after separation, incapacity or death only with qualified local advice. Account ownership, community-property rules, debts, taxes and estate documents vary. A meeting can identify the question; it should not invent the law.
The account structure passes when shared bills are reliable, both partners retain appropriate agency, emergency access is lawful and no one must surrender all privacy to prove commitment.

Choose how income changes affect contributions before the change arrives. A proportional formula can adjust automatically, while equal-dollar funding may be simpler. Either can be fair when caregiving, benefits and unpaid work are considered openly. Revisit after leave, unemployment, disability, promotion or self-employment rather than letting an outdated split create silent resentment.

sections.heading: Turn Goals into Trade-Offs Both Partners Can See
paragraphs: Goals compete for the same cash and time. Name the outcome, target amount, target date, current balance, monthly contribution and owner. “Buy a home” becomes useful only when deposit, closing costs, location, timing and the effect on other priorities are visible.

Ask each partner to rank goals independently before negotiating. A ranking reveals intensity that a combined brainstorm hides. Discuss why the top item matters—security, family, freedom, identity or enjoyment—before moving numbers.

[[S5|FDIC guidance]] recommends reviewing spending and using regular automatic transfers to build savings. Automation is effective only after both partners approve the amount and the operating account can support the date.

Create a household priority stack with one stability goal, one growth goal and one quality-of-life goal. Funding every aspiration equally can leave all of them too slow to motivate. Concentration should be time-bounded and reviewed.

Use trade-off sentences: “If we add $300 to travel, the debt payoff moves two months,” or “If we keep the date, the target purchase must shrink.” A transparent consequence is easier to negotiate than an accusation about values.

Value unpaid labor and capacity. A side job, home renovation or aggressive savings target may consume evenings, childcare and recovery. Record who absorbs that cost. A plan is not jointly chosen if one person receives the goal and the other receives all implementation work.

Protect individual goals within reason. Education, family support, creative work or personal safety savings may matter even when they do not maximize a shared spreadsheet. Agree on boundaries rather than requiring identical priorities.

Use a minimum, target and stretch contribution. The minimum maintains progress during a difficult month; the target fits the normal plan; the stretch uses genuine surplus. This avoids treating one missed target as permission to abandon the goal.

Celebrate milestones without raiding the progress. Choose a small, planned recognition or a nonfinancial reward. The meeting should create evidence that cooperation improves life, not only that it limits spending.

The goal section passes when both partners can explain the top priorities, monthly amount, trade-off and review date. Agreement does not require equal enthusiasm; it requires informed consent to the plan.

Separate the goal from its funding account. A shared vacation can be funded from individual contributions, a joint savings account or an institution subaccount, each with different access and ownership. Labeling money does not change the contract. Choose the legal structure deliberately and keep the goal tracker from implying rights the account agreement does not provide.

When partners cannot rank two goals, test a temporary allocation rather than demanding permanent philosophical agreement. Fund each at a stated ratio for three months, observe motivation and cash strain, then review. A reversible experiment can produce better evidence than an abstract debate about which value should govern every future dollar.

sections.heading: Protect the Conversation from Control and Escalation
paragraphs: Financial disagreement is normal. Financial control is not. Restricting access to essentials, hiding or confiscating income, coerced signatures, debt opened without consent, threats tied to money or monitoring that creates fear can indicate abuse. A standard joint-budget exercise may increase danger.

If safety is in question, use a private device where possible and seek confidential support before changing accounts. An abuser may monitor browser history, location, mail or transactions. Do not confront suspected fraud or move money if doing so creates immediate risk without a safety plan.

For ordinary conflict, use a pause protocol: either person says “pause,” names a return time within a reasonable window and records the unresolved decision. A pause ends escalation; it does not let a partner avoid every required bill indefinitely.

Speak from observable facts and needs: “The card statement is $600 above our plan, and rent clears Friday” rather than “You never care.” Ask what happened, listen to the answer and separate a one-time exception from a recurring rule problem.

The conflict photograph belongs earlier in the body because money stress is a predictable system condition, not a dramatic ending. Recognizing posture, tone and shutdown allows a couple to stop before a financial question becomes a relationship injury.

Use thresholds to prevent repeated permission-seeking: purchases above an amount, new debt, family transfers, subscription commitments and account openings require prior discussion. Below-threshold personal spending stays personal when the plan is funded.

When a mistake occurs, define repair: reverse or return if possible, fund the gap, correct automation, notify an institution, and change the rule that failed. Punishment without process improvement leaves the next error intact.

Bring in a qualified counselor, mediator, tax professional, attorney or fiduciary adviser when the issue exceeds the couple’s expertise or communication capacity. Choose the professional jointly where safe and clarify confidentiality and fees.

Never use financial literacy as a weapon. One partner’s technical knowledge does not create unilateral authority, and the less experienced partner should have time and independent explanation before signing a material contract.
The conflict system passes when either person can raise a concern without fear, pauses have return dates, safety overrides forced transparency and material decisions receive genuine consent.

Privacy is not identical to secrecy. Agreed personal spending, confidential therapy or a lawful safety reserve can coexist with honest disclosure of material obligations. Secrecy becomes a household issue when hidden debt, income, assets or commitments change shared risk. Define the boundary prospectively and symmetrically instead of deciding it only after a disputed transaction.

sections.heading: End with Owners, Deadlines and Verification
paragraphs: Every decision needs five fields: action, amount or scope, owner, deadline and proof. “We will save more” fails all five. “Asha schedules a $150 transfer from household checking on each payday and both verify the first transfer Friday” can be implemented.

Distribute ownership instead of assigning one permanent household chief financial officer. One person may execute bills while the other reconciles, researches insurance or maintains the document inventory. Rotate enough work that both can operate the system during an emergency.

Use institution automation for approved repetitive actions and calendar tasks for variable work. Automation should not conceal activity. Both partners need alerts for low balance, large transactions, failed payments and material account changes where available.

The late photograph shows a different couple collaborating over documents and a laptop because the desired outcome is not perfect agreement; it is coordinated execution. Placement here connects the article’s final phase to shared follow-through rather than conflict.

Maintain a one-page decision log: date, facts reviewed, decision, dissent or condition, owner, deadline and status. Do not store unnecessary sensitive data. The log prevents the same issue from being renegotiated from memory each month.

Hold a fifteen-minute weekly check for immediate balances and bills, a monthly decision meeting, and a longer quarterly or annual review for insurance, taxes, beneficiaries, credit, retirement and estate questions. Cadence should match complexity.

Reconcile automation after the first cycle. Confirm that transfers posted, payments drew from the intended account, income arrived and goal balances changed. A confirmation screen is not proof that a scheduled instruction settled.

At the next meeting, review overdue actions before opening new topics. Ask whether the task was unclear, too large, blocked or assigned unfairly. Redesign the system rather than treating every missed task as lack of commitment.
Archive completed meeting notes securely and delete obsolete exports containing sensitive data. Update the emergency contact and account inventory when ownership or access changes.

The money meeting is complete when the household has shared facts, a small set of decisions, lawful access, named owners and a verification date. Repeatability matters more than intensity: a calm monthly system outperforms one heroic annual argument.

Create a contingency rule for missed meetings. Essential bills and previously approved automation continue, but new discretionary commitments above the threshold wait unless both agree through a documented channel. Reschedule within a set window. This prevents avoidance from freezing operations and prevents one partner from using urgency to bypass the agreed decision process.

Once a year, test the system as if the usual money manager were unavailable for thirty days. The backup partner should locate bills, insurance, tax records, account contacts and the decision log without needing passwords they are not authorized to use. Record the gaps and fix access through lawful institution features, not credential sharing.

summary: A productive couple’s money meeting is scheduled, bounded and collaborative. Agree on the purpose, agenda, time and pause rules before discussing numbers. Do not begin during a purchase dispute or use the meeting to audit one partner’s character.

Prepare a shared snapshot of income, balances, debts, bills, insurance, taxes, upcoming irregular expenses and goals. Record ownership and access accurately without placing passwords, identity documents or full account numbers in an insecure spreadsheet.

Use an agenda that moves from facts to decisions: check-in, changes, balances, upcoming bills, exceptions, one priority choice, assigned actions and next date. Limit complex meetings to one major decision so agreement can become execution.

Build cash flow by pay and bill date rather than monthly average. Include an operating buffer and sinking funds for annual insurance, repairs, school, medical and other predictable irregular costs. Give every bill before the next meeting a funding source.

Discuss debt as a contract. List borrower, balance, rate, minimum, due date, promotion, collateral and delinquency. Keep required minimums current, choose one extra-payment rule and distinguish legal responsibility from voluntary household support.

Joint, separate and hybrid account structures can all work. Evaluate reliable bill funding, lawful emergency access, personal autonomy and ownership consequences. Joint-account holders can often withdraw or close funds under the agreement, so ownership should never be added casually.

Give each partner agreed personal spending that does not require transaction-level approval. Set thresholds for major purchases, new debt, subscriptions and family transfers. Shared planning should reduce surveillance rather than normalize it.

Turn goals into target amount, date, monthly contribution and trade-off. Rank goals independently, then choose a stability, growth and quality-of-life priority. Account for the unpaid time and caregiving required to implement each plan.

Ordinary conflict needs a pause-and-return process. Financial abuse, coerced debt, blocked access or fear requires confidential safety and legal support, not forced transparency. Never pressure someone to share accounts when disclosure may create danger.

End every decision with action, amount, owner, deadline and proof. Use automation for stable approved tasks, alerts for exceptions and a concise decision log. Verify that instructions settled instead of trusting submission screens.

Use a short weekly operations check, a monthly decision meeting and a deeper periodic review for taxes, insurance, beneficiaries, credit and long-term goals. Review overdue actions before adding new ones and redistribute household financial labor when needed.

The system works when both partners can explain the household, meet ordinary bills, retain appropriate agency and continue operations during illness or absence. Calm repetition and verified follow-through matter more than one perfect budget.

Define the meeting’s boundaries. Record connected relationship, parenting, legal or tax questions that need another setting, but do not let them consume the operational agenda. Rotating facilitator and note-taking roles helps distribute the mental work and prevents financial fluency from becoming unilateral authority.

Reconcile account transfers consistently so card payments and savings movements are not counted twice. Distinguish primary borrowers, joint owners, authorized users and beneficiaries. Visibility, access, ownership and liability are different concepts, and changing a household spreadsheet does not change an institution’s contract.

Agree in advance how income changes affect shared contributions. Revisit the formula after leave, job loss, promotion, disability, caregiving or self-employment. Equal dollars, proportional income and other methods can work when benefits and unpaid labor are considered openly and the rule applies fairly.

Test continuity annually by asking the backup partner to operate essential finances for thirty days. They should locate due dates, policy contacts, tax records and approved actions using lawful access. Repair missing documentation and institution permissions without exchanging insecure credentials.

When two goals remain tied, run a short reversible funding experiment with a stated ratio and review date. Evidence from actual cash flow and motivation can resolve a trade-off more constructively than demanding permanent agreement during one meeting.

faq.question: How long should a first money meeting last?
faq.answer: Use a bounded session, often 30–45 minutes, with one major decision and a scheduled follow-up.

faq.question: Must couples combine every account?
faq.answer: No. Joint, separate and hybrid structures can work when bills, access, ownership and autonomy are explicit.

faq.question: What information should both partners know?
faq.answer: Income, bills, major assets and debts, insurance, taxes, goals, ownership, due dates and emergency contacts.

faq.question: Should partners share banking passwords?
faq.answer: Use institution-supported access and individual credentials rather than exchanging or reusing passwords.

faq.question: What if the conversation becomes heated?
faq.answer: Pause, record the unresolved decision and set a return time; seek qualified help for recurring escalation.

faq.question: What makes a meeting actionable?
faq.answer: Every decision receives an amount or scope, owner, deadline and method of verification.

glossary.definition: A date-based view of income, bills, saving and available balances.
Money accumulated gradually for a known but irregular future expense.
A minimum checking balance used to absorb timing variation and small errors.
An account legally owned under an agreement by more than one account holder.
A person permitted to use an account without necessarily becoming an owner or primary borrower.
A person or organization designated to receive specified assets or proceeds.
An agreed amount or category requiring discussion before commitment.
A concise record of an agreed action, owner, deadline and verification status.
